question: A photo app sorts each picture into one group, such as "cat" or "dog". Which computer vision task is this?
incorrectAnswers: Object detection
Image segmentation
Optical character recognition
explanation: Image classification puts a whole image into one of a set of predefined classes. It says what the picture shows, but not where in the picture it is.

question: What does object detection add on top of simply naming what is in an image?
correctAnswer: Where each object is, marked with a box
incorrectAnswers: A sharper, higher-resolution copy of the image
A caption describing the mood of the scene
The camera settings used to take the photo
explanation: Object detection combines classification with localization: it names each object and draws a bounding box around it. That lets a system count objects or follow them, not just label the scene.

question: When grading an object detector, what does the "intersection over union" score check?
correctAnswer: How well a predicted box overlaps the correct box
incorrectAnswers: How quickly the model processes each frame
How many objects the model finds per image
How bright the image is inside each box
explanation: The score is the overlapping area of the two boxes divided by their combined area. A detection usually counts as correct only when the label is right and this overlap passes a set threshold.

question: Why might a team randomly flip, rotate and crop its training photos before training an image model?
correctAnswer: To add realistic variety so the model copes with new photos
incorrectAnswers: To shrink the dataset so training finishes sooner
To hide the labels so the model has to guess
To make every photo look exactly the same
explanation: This is called data augmentation. Small random but realistic changes make the training set more varied without collecting new photos, and they are applied only during training.

question: A team has only about 120 photos of each insect type. What common approach helps them still build a good classifier?
correctAnswer: Fine-tune a model already trained on a huge image set
incorrectAnswers: Train a brand-new model from random starting weights
Train only on the photos' file names and dates
Shrink every photo to a single pixel first
explanation: This is transfer learning. Very few people train a vision network from scratch, because that needs a very large dataset; reusing a network pretrained on millions of images lets a small dataset go much further.

question: In a typical color photo, each pixel is stored as three numbers. What do those three numbers describe?
correctAnswer: How much red, green and blue light it has
incorrectAnswers: Its brightness, contrast and sharpness
Its width, height and depth on screen
Its hue, shadow and focus level
explanation: Colors on screens are made by mixing red, green and blue light. Each of the three values is commonly stored with 8 bits, giving a whole number from 0 to 255.

question: When a computer "looks" at a digital photo, what is it actually working with?
correctAnswer: A grid of pixels, each stored as numbers
incorrectAnswers: A list of the objects the photo contains
A text description saved by the camera
A set of curved lines and filled shapes
explanation: A digital image has a fixed number of rows and columns of pixels, stored as an array of small whole numbers. Each number records brightness or color at one point, so image AI starts from numbers, not objects.

question: Why does an image classifier usually need a large, varied set of labelled photos?
correctAnswer: Small or narrow datasets rarely show reliable patterns
incorrectAnswers: Labels make the photos smaller to store
Large datasets remove the need for any testing
Varied photos let the model run without a computer chip
explanation: A label is the correct answer the model learns to predict, such as "tulip". Most models cannot find reliable patterns in a small dataset, and a big dataset still needs variety to cover real-world cases.

question: A famous research dataset has over 14 million labelled images. How were most of those labels created?
correctAnswer: Crowd workers labelled them by hand online
incorrectAnswers: A computer program labelled them automatically
They were copied from each image's file name
Photographers tagged them when taking the shots
explanation: The ImageNet project crowdsourced its annotation, using paid online workers to say which objects appeared in each image. It shows how much human effort sits behind the labelled data that image AI learns from.

question: In 2012, what type of model won a major image recognition contest by a margin of more than 10 percentage points?
incorrectAnswers: A decision tree
A hand-written rule system
A large language model
explanation: The network known as AlexNet reached a 15.3% top-5 error in the 2012 ImageNet challenge, more than 10.8 points better than the runner-up. The result drew wide attention to deep learning for images.

question: In a convolutional neural network for images, what do the first layers typically react to?
correctAnswer: Simple features such as edges and color blobs
incorrectAnswers: Whole objects such as faces and cars
The photo's file name and capture date
Full sentences describing the scene
explanation: Small filters slide across the image and fire on simple patterns like edges. Deeper layers combine these over wider areas to recognize larger, more complex shapes.

question: Compared with drawing a box around each object, what does image segmentation give you?
correctAnswer: The exact outline of objects, pixel by pixel
incorrectAnswers: One label that describes the whole photo
A sharper version of the original photo
A written caption for each object found
explanation: Segmentation is a more precise, pixel-level version of object detection. Tracing exact shapes is useful in tasks like outlining a tumor in a medical scan.

question: A phone app reads the text on a photographed receipt so you can copy it. What is this technology called?
incorrectAnswers: Facial recognition
Image segmentation
Data augmentation
explanation: Optical character recognition (OCR) turns images of printed or handwritten text into machine-readable text. It is also used to read passports, license plates and scanned documents.

question: What is the difference between face detection and face recognition?
correctAnswer: Detection finds a face; recognition works out whose it is
incorrectAnswers: Detection works the person out; recognition only finds the face
Detection works only on video; recognition only on photos
Detection needs color images; recognition needs black and white
explanation: A recognition system first detects the face to separate it from the background. It then turns the face into features and matches them against a database of known faces.
